text: Oicatá is a town and municipality located in the Central Boyacá Province, Department of Boyacá, Colombia. Its urban centre lies on the Altiplano Cundiboyacense at an altitude of 2,815 metres (9,236 ft), approximately 153 kilometres (95 mi) from Bogotá and 15 kilometres (9.3 mi) from Tunja, the department capital. It shares borders with Cómbita and Tuta to the north, Chivatá and Tunja to the south, Chivatá to the east, and Cómbita and Tunja to the west. The name Oicatá derives from the Chibcha language and means "Domain of the priests" or "Hailstoned farmlands." The municipality was established on May 9, 1539, by Pedro Ruiz Corredor. Prior to the Spanish conquest, the area belonged to the Muisca, the most advanced society in Colombia in terms of social, cultural, and productive development. After the conquest, governance was carried out by the Governor General, appointed directly by the King of Spain. The people achieved independence from Spain following the Battle of Boyacá on August 7, 1819, where Simón Bolívar's forces defeated Spanish troops. In 1821, the Constitution of Cúcuta introduced a hierarchical administrative structure, dividing the country into departments, provinces, counties, and parishes, and established Boyacá Department as comprising the provinces of Tunja, Pamplona, Socorro, and Casanare. The Act of June 15, 1857, declared Boyacá a sovereign state including the provinces of Tunja, Tundama, Casanare, and the counties of Chiquinquirá and Velez. The Act of October 31 of that year created four departments: Tunja with 42 districts, Tundama with 46, Casanare with 21, and Oriente (East) with 6. Under the Constitution of Rionegro in 1863, administrative divisions were modified, and Law 10 of that year reorganized Boyacá into six departments: Casanare, Tundama, North, West, East, and Centre. The centrist Constitution of 1886 established a structure of departments, provinces, and municipalities. In 1911, Executive Decree No. 306 abolished provinces and led to the creation of the commissariat of Arauca from several municipalities. Subsequently, municipalities in the Orinoco region formed the intendency of Casanare as part of Boyacá until 1973, when it separated again. The primary economic activity in Oicatá is agriculture, producing potatoes, maize, barley, wheat, peas, and beans. The climate of Oicatá is influenced by its location and altitude, with an elevation of nearly 3,000 metres, making it one of Colombia’s higher cities. It has a subtropical highland climate (Köppen Cfb) characterized by minimal temperature variation year-round and a distinct dry season from December to February.
